Using a logistic regression model with age as the only predictor, the predicted probability of achieving efficacy PR with treatment in a patient aged 65 is approximately 0.40 (39.5%, 95% CI ≈ 27.3%–53.2% by the delta method). The model was PR (1) vs non-PR (0) ~ Age, fit by maximum likelihood on all 80 treated patients in data/data.xlsx (Sheet1). Age was significantly inversely associated with achieving PR: log-OR = −0.075 per year (OR = 0.93 per year, 95% CI 0.88–0.97, p = 0.002), so older patients have a lower predicted probability of PR.

Key details:
- Data: 121 sheet rows reduced to 80 real patients (41 trailing fully blank rows dropped; one whitespace-only cell treated as missing). Among the 80 patients there were no missing values in Age, Groups, or Efficacy.
- Concordance check: Groups perfectly partitions Efficacy — Group 1 (n=41) all 'PR'; Group 2 (n=39) 'SD' (17) or 'PD' (22), zero PR. Binary outcome = Efficacy == 'PR' (SD and PD both counted as non-PR); results are identical whether the outcome is defined from Efficacy or from Groups.
- Model: logit(p) = 4.4466 − 0.0750·Age; at Age = 65, linear predictor = −0.428 → p = 0.395. Sanity check: observed PR rate among patients aged 60–70 (n=23) was 26%, consistent with a prediction below 50% in that range.
- Caveat noted in the deliverable: if "treatment" were interpreted as Group 1 only, the outcome is constant (41/41 PR) and an Age-only logistic regression is degenerate; the non-degenerate reading (all 80 patients as the treated cohort, PR vs SD/PD) was used, per the approved plan.
